articles.title_orig: Dow futures surge 900 points after decisive win by Democrats in U.S. midterms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures surge 900 points after decisive win by Democrats in U.S. midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures ripped higher on Wednesday as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections — and President Donald Trump's acceptance of the results — removed political uncertainty risk hanging over Wall Street.
Democrats won majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, and scored victories in key gubernatorial races like Texas. The Democrats will now be a check on the policies of Trump, who's enacted business-friendly tax cuts, while also pursuing tariffs and a war in Iran that's boosted inflation.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 912 points, or 1.75%. S&P 500 futures traded 0.8% higher. Nasdaq-100 futures were on weakness in AI-related stocks.
Trump told the New York Times he was "absolutely willing" to accept the results and told the Wall Street Journal he and Republicans would work with Democrats.
The rebound "was in part due to the president's initial tone and reaction to the results," said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. "Still more uncertainty looms, but one thing is certain, there will be gridlock and historically this is good for the market."
Shares linked to the economy that could benefit from a more stable environment led the early gains. Walmart added 2%, while Bank of America rose 1.9% as investors looked for stocks outside of technology.
Shares that could benefit directly from Democratic policies, or an end to tougher Trump actions, gained. Health insurers and hospital operators advanced, with United Health up 1.4%, Molina Healthcare rising 6.3%, Centene adding 4.7% and HCA Healthcare up 1.44%. The Invesco Solar ETF jumped 5%.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Investors feared a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. The Texas governor win by Gina Hinojosa, who's pledged an immediate moratorium in the key data center hub, added to the fears Wednesday.
Shares of Oracle and CoreWeave were headed lower Wednesday, along with Elon Musk's SpaceX , which is headquartered in Texas.
Another reason for the bullish sentiment Wednesday morning was that history shows the market does well under a divided government , where fewer policies and regulations are able to interfere with the business outlook.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe", Slimmon also said that if the result increases the push for a resolution to the Middle East conflict, that may bring oil prices lower.  "That's been an issue for the Fed, and inflation, and part of the reason that rates are higher."
WTI crude oil prices were 1% lower on Wednesday.

Private-sector job growth held steady in October, with gains spread across sectors, as the labor market showed fresh signs of stabilization, ADP reported Wednesday.
The payrolls processing firm said companies added 86,000 jobs during the month, the same as the downwardly revised total for September and slightly ahead of the Dow Jones estimate for 75,000.
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.
U.S. renewable energy stocks climbed on expectations of a policy shift. First Solar advanced 8.5%, Bloom Energy gained 5.8%, Plug Power rose 10.6%, Sunrun notched an 8.64% gain, FuelCell Energy was up 6.24% and SolarEdge Technologies moved 4% higher.
Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.
European renewable energy stocks moved sharply higher in early trade as prospects of a decisive Democrat victory in the U.S. midterm elections sparked hopes of a U.S. policy shift on renewables.
Copenhagen-listed Oersted surged 7.3% while Danish peer Vestas advanced 5.2%. The two companies have grappled with uncertainty in their U.S. businesses in recent years, partly as a result of fierce opposition from the Trump administration toward the renewable energy sector.
SMA Solar shares were up 5.5% and Nordex shares added 4.8%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.44% in early trading, as the continent's stocks and major bourses moved higher on the Democrats' clean sweep of the U.S. midterms.
Banks advanced 1.83%, leading gains, with basic resources up 1.71% and utilities rising 0.68%. Food and beverage stocks lost 0.57%, and industrial goods fell 0.37%.
The Italian FTSE MIB was up 0.88%, leading regional bourses. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.22%, while the French CAC 40 rose 0.24% and Germany's DAX gained 0.28%.
Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates amid continued GLP-1 volume growth globally, sending shares up as much as 6% in early trading.
The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.
Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year at constant exchange rates and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
It comes as the Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed Wednesday, as investors assessed a projected Democratic takeover of the U.S. Senate and House, while President Donald Trump appeared to not challenge the results.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.62% to end at 5,683.8, while the small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq added 1.5% to 714.95 in choppy trading.
Japan's Nikkei 225 pared some losses to close 1.42% lower at 62,188.63, and the broad-based Topix declined 0.89% to 3,895.38.
Mainland China's CSI 300 gained 2.31% to 4,101.34, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.43% higher in its last hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.59% to 8,834.5.
— Lee Ying Shan, Lim Hui Jie
The dollar moved lower against most major currencies as the Democrats took control of Congress after the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro was last seen 0.39% higher against the dollar at $1.1235, while the British pound also strengthened against the greenback, rising 0.48% to $1.3476.

articles.title_orig: US midterms: What Trump's defeat means for Europe and global markets
articles.title_zh: US midterms: What Trump's defeat means for Europe and global markets
articles.content_orig:
With Democrats in power, Trump may be under siege and lose his dominance over the Republican party – but his id will relish at the prospect of fighting
US midterms 2026 live – latest updates
Tell us: what do you want to know about the midterm election results?
Donald Trump posted a document on social media this summer by a supposed historian that compared him with, among others, Napoleon Bonaparte and Adolf Hitler. That now seems fitting: the US president has himself fought one battle too many, and appears to have brought about his own destruction.
Tuesday’s US midterm elections were a thumping, shellacking and extinction-level event rolled into one. Ruby-red Republican strongholds once deemed safe toppled like dominoes. Democrats won Senate seats for the first time in Kansas since 1932, in Texas since 1988 and in South Carolina since 1998.
The House of Representatives and Senate had flipped from one party to the other in the same midterm just three times since the second world war – in 1946, 1994 and 2006 – but now it has happened again, ensuring that the US Congress will be a bulwark against Trump’s expansion of executive power.
The president, who swiftly noted he was not on the ticket on Tuesday, is the architect of his own lame duck status. Indeed, having spent months repeatedly urging voters to pretend he was on the ticket, he could hardly have done any more to sabotage his own party. In 2024 he won the presidency promising to lower prices and end foreign wars; his tariffs added to upward pressure on prices, and his ill-starred attack on Iran pushed them higher still.
Then there was Trump’s wild and bizarre campaign, which consisted of long and rambling speeches about architectural projects, outbursts of vile Islamophobia and musings about the “ass” of a Republican senator from Ohio. It culminated at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, where he declared victory in the war on algae.
The voters said: enough is enough.
Now for the Republican postmortem. According to exit polls from the Associated Press, voters said the cost of living and government corruption were their two top issues. Trump, who was purported to be an economic populist, had flaunted his self-enrichment and fancy ballroom even as people struggled to put food on the table. It was too much even for some in his supposedly rock-solid base.
How will Trump cope with this new political reality? Is this the beginning of the end?
From January, Democrats will have the power to block legislation, launch investigations into Trump’s administration and thwart his judicial and senior government appointments. Life could suddenly become uncomfortable for the likes of Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, or Big Tech leaders such as Elon Musk. Democrats might even consider impeaching Trump for a third time.
That potentially leaves the president under siege – a diminished figure mired in Washington gridlock and reduced to wielding a veto pen, which he had already starting threatening to use on Tuesday evening.
However, it must be said that Trump paid little attention to Congress during his first two years in office, apart from the passage of his Big, Beautiful Act of tax and spending measures . He has acted unilaterally on tariffs and military strikes on Venezuela and Iran. Like his predecessors, he will surely continue to pursue foreign policy as a legacy project, an alarming prospect for the world.
He will also push on with his other obsession: giving Washington a radical makeover with a new White House ballroom, a triumphal arch and more gold. Congress might take the view that this is a relatively harmless activity to keep him occupied compared to the havoc he could be wreaking elsewhere.
More threatening to Trump than any Democratic investigation is the inexorable march of time. The race to succeed him in 2028 begins now.
This president is psychologically ill-equipped to deal with the prospect of the national spotlight leaving him to focus on JD Vance, Marco Rubio and other potential candidates.
That shift could also eat away at Trump’s cult-like dominance of the Republican party and the Maga movement. He has shaped the party in his own image for a decade and it will not easily snap back. But members of Congress picking through the wreckage of Tuesday may well conclude that Trump is a creature of the past – and their survival depends on placing the right bets on the future.
Every swing of the electoral pendulum gets over-interpreted. Trump’s two presidential election victories were seen as a fundamental shift in America, even though he never achieved 50% of the national popular vote. His defeat in 2020 was hailed as the end of the Trump era, only for him to rise from the political dead four years later.
Anyone re-proclaiming the end of that era after Tuesday’s landslide should remember that the president is not yet halfway through his second term, and that his id will relish the prospect of fighting Democrats.
A wounded Trump who feels he has nothing to lose over the next two years might turn out to be the most reckless and dangerous of all.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu's claim of vote fraud
articles.title_zh: Israel’s president accepts certified election results in a blow to Netanyahu's claim of vote fraud
articles.content_orig:
Move comes after attorney general blocks Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties
Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel .
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu, so they are expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title_orig: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.title_zh: Switch 1 & 2 Cartridges Under Threat As Key ROM Manufacturer Exits Business
articles.content_orig:
Macronix, one of Nintendo's key ROM manufacturers for physical game cartridges, is ceasing the production of ROM altogether.
This comes via analyst David Gibson who relayed the news from Macronix's latest financial release. According to the data, ROM products accounted for just 5% of the firm's overall revenue for Q3 2026, representing a stark decrease of 39% year-on-year.
It will now shift its focus over to NOR and eMMC memory chips instead, and will no longer report ROM sales separately in its future financial releases.
Gibson is keen to stress that Nintendo will have other partners to utilise when it comes to the production of cartridges, but this move may nevertheless accelerate the transition to digital game sales alongside Game-Key Cards.
Digital sales have already made up more than 60% of Nintendo's total sales during Q4 2026 and Q1 2027, but this tends to fluctuate based on major game releases.
It'll be interesting to see whether Nintendo itself addresses this development in its own financial release, which it due to drop this week on 5th November. Even if it doesn't acknowledge it in its own material, it seems likely that the question will arise in the company's usual Q&A session. We'll keep an eye out and relay its reaction and plans going forward.
For now, it's likely business as usual for Nintendo, but we'll be interested to see just how this affects the production of physical cartridges in the future and whether it will indeed accelerate the transition to digital.

articles.title_orig: CVS to Split off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.title_zh: CVS to Split off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.content_orig:

CVS ( CVS ) announced plans to separate into two independent, publicly traded companies on Wednesday, reshaping one of the largest healthcare companies in the US.
The company intends to separate CVS Health's insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and healthcare services operations from its retail pharmacy and community healthcare segments.
The planned separation represents a significant shift from CVS Health's long-term strategy of bringing together insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and direct healthcare services under a single corporate structure.
Under the proposed structure, one company will retain the CVS Health name and house Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.
The second entity, which will operate under the name CVS Pharmacy, will include approximately 9,000 retail pharmacy locations and MinuteClinic locations, among other services.
Management believes that separating the businesses will allow each organization to operate with greater independence while maintaining the ability to pursue partnerships across the healthcare industry.
The planned separation is expected to be completed in the first half of 2028
On Wednesday, CVS also reported third quarter results with total revenue increasing 5.4% year over year to $108.4 billion, compared with $102.9 billion in the prior-year period. Adjusted earnings per share rose to $2.09 from $1.60 a year earlier.
Following the quarterly performance, CVS raised its full-year 2026 financial guidance, now expecting adjusted earnings per share of at least $8.20, compared with its previous range of $7.90 to $8.10.
Shares of CVS dropped roughly 2% in premarket trading. The stock is up roughly 15% year-to-date.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s Q3 sales seen slowing as spending cools, now value, drinks in focus
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s Q3 sales seen slowing as spending cools, now value, drinks in focus
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
McDonald's ( MCD ) sales growth slowed in the third quarter as consumers faced a challenging economic backdrop and the fast food chain unveiled its growth strategy. The results showed that same-store sales grew by 1.5% year over year, a tick above the 1.4% growth Wall Street expected, according to Bloomberg estimates. In Q3 last year, McDonald's posted same-store sales growth of 3.6%.
In the US, the company posted a 0.2% decline in comparable sales, slightly narrower than the expected 0.5% drop. Data from Placer.ai showed visits to the Golden Arches declined from a year ago, but the company said customers spent more when they did go. Promotions in October led to some strength ahead of the holiday season. CEO Chris Kempczinski said the company is "encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value."
Revenue came in at nearly $7.2 billion, below expectations of $7.4 billion, alongside adjusted earnings of $3.57 per share, above the expected $3.40 per share.
Ahead of the results, BTIG analyst Peter Saleh said "lower-income challenges, disappointing promotions and overly crowded marketing calendars" were top concerns among franchisee operators in the quarter.
"Beverages were called out as a rare bright spot," he added, alluding to an energy drink McDonald's launched with Red Bull in September.
The company is also leaning into holiday offerings beginning on Nov. 3. McDonald's unveiled a limited-time lineup consisting of a cookie butter coffee or latte, a cranberry-infused Sprite drink, and a cranberry-flavored Red Bull energy drink.
Citi's Jon Tower shared a similar message in a note, writing, "We still have confidence in beverages as a broader platform, [and] another attempt at entry-level value should come in early '27."
The company named Skye Anderson, a 26-year McDonald's veteran, as president of McDonald's USA last quarter. Anderson is working on a new value menu for 2027 after franchisees and consumers didn't fully engage with the company's under-$3 offerings.
Anderson will play a key role in a new growth strategy as McDonald's makes a long-term bet on artificial intelligence, hand-breaded chicken, and a return of the 90s-style restaurant design to regain customers who left for other chains, like Burger King ( QSR ).
McDonald's said it plans to invest $8.5 billion through 2036 to support restaurant tech updates with rent relief and capital. It intends to deliver roughly $5 billion of that investment by 2030.
According to Saleh, franchisees' reactions to the NEXT growth strategy are mixed.
"Franchisees [are] highly skeptical that level of margin gain is possible, unconvinced a broad remodel program is needed, and noting very few details about cost and co-investment have been shared," Saleh wrote. "Without a significant reduction in build cost and more field-testing, we don't believe Project NEXT can proceed."
McDonald's operators are expected to update the restaurants' look and feel as part of a 10-year remodel cycle, per McDonald's, and Kempczinski said those costs typically add up to $400,000 to $450,000 per restaurant.
Deploying the suite of McDonald's productivity improvements will cost franchise operators an additional $800,000 per US restaurant. For international markets, it will run operators around $650,000 to $750,000.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices to Come Under Pressure if Midterms Outcome Halts Iran Escalation
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices to Come Under Pressure if Midterms Outcome Halts Iran Escalation
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

With only a couple of seats left to be called in the midterm elections, a “blue wave” is preparing to wash through Congress. Voters made it clear they were unhappy with Republicans in the first two years of President Trump’s administration, with 54 Democrats elected to the Senate and 44 Republicans, as of this writing, per CNBC . Consumers will want to see action on issues close to home from their newly elected officials, namely affordability and inflation . Military conflict with Iran has pushed up oil prices and, as a result, gas prices. That action came after Trump’s tariff scheme, which targeted exports from foreign countries, but economists say it resulted in increased costs being passed back to consumers.
While Main Street has a checklist of action it wants to see, Wall Street is hedging on how the new power dynamics on Capitol Hill will play out.
In the early hours of this morning, yields on longer-dated bonds trended downward as demand inversely rose. 30-Year Treasuries pushed below 5.3%, while the 10-year pushed down toward 4.9%.
Demand for the securities shows bonds remain the destination of choice in a market flight to safety—a question which seemed to hang over the market this summer as yields rose over 5%.
A more divided government increases the likelihood of government standoffs, particularly over spending. “Fiscal gridlock seems the likely default,” UBS’s Paul Donovan told clients this morning. “President Trump has seemingly retreated from an earlier pledge to veto everything the Democrats suggest, Treasuries have initially strengthened on the results.”
Beyond a shield against volatility, investors have additional motivations to look to bonds in the current political climate. President Trump and his team may now find it harder to push through policy packages that might require more spending and, as a result, more government borrowing. Likewise, Democrat spending packages could face roadblocks from a still sizeable Republican presence in Congress and Trump’s veto power.
Markets are also bracing for near-term volatility in equities, as UBS’s chief investment officer, Mark Haefele, noted to clients, “particularly in tech and other areas sensitive to greater regulatory scrutiny.” With AI driving stock gains this year, investors may seek to balance any hiccups with the dependable asset of Treasuries.
While spending gridlock may frustrate policymakers, it might calm the nerves of debt hawks. Concern over the fiscal trajectory of the U.S. is mounting, owing to federal deficits of between 6% and 7% of GDP, and interest payments on the national debt now demand more than $1 trillion a year.
A gridlock could slow the path of any spending bills, allaying some concerns about the U.S. budget picture. As Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noted this morning: “There’s been a rally for U.S. Treasuries … given that divided government has generally made it harder for fiscal stimulus to be passed. So that’s eased concerns on the fiscal trajectory a bit.”
Policymakers’ appetite for a conversation on fiscal responsibility may be gauged sooner rather than later. The current federal government funding package runs out on December 11 and will require bipartisan support to prevent a government shutdown.
While the officials elected in the midterms won’t be in office until the New Year, a shift in the tide may give Democrats more motivation to hold the line or make bolder demands in return for support.
The odds of a government shutdown jumped to 45% overnight on the prediction market platform Kalshi , up from around 30%.

articles.content_orig:
A large-scale watering hole attack associated with Russian hackers has been targeting iOS and Android users visiting compromised sites or fake ones impersonating legitimate portals.
The campaign used multiple high-profile websites in the U.S., Ukraine, the Czech Republic, and Bulgaria that delivered the same payload for profiling visitors and their devices.
This initial stage allows the attacker to determine the browser version to deploy "platform-specific n-day exploit chains without user interaction."
Researchers at cybersecurity company Sekoia attribute the operation with moderate-to-high confidence to APT29 (aka Midnight Blizzard), a Russian threat group that was recently linked to hotel WiFi attacks .
Based on their findings, compromised legitimate sites belong to a Ukrainian gas producer, a U.S. chemical industry trade association, and a Bulgarian military-related site.
Lookalike domains impersonated the official America250 site and Raffles London at The OWO hotel, relaying content from the real sites in an adversary-in-the-middle attack model.
The researchers also discovered that the threat actor had compromised Ukrainian web analytics service Plerdy and modified its SEO tracker, which was loaded by thousands of websites, mostly in Ukraine, between August 27 and September 3.
In all cases, the initial payload was JavaScript code that profiled website visitors to determine their devices and browser versions. The command-and-control (C2) server then pushed the correct exploit chain.
According to Sekoia, the threat actors exploited the following vulnerabilities to extract cookies, messaging app databases, and credentials:
The researchers identified four other vulnerabilities in unreachable code or alternate exploit paths, but they were not used in the analyzed chains.
CVE-2025-43529 is linked to the “DarkSword” exploit kit , first documented in March, and leveraged in attacks since at least November 2025 by multiple threat groups.
Sekoia says that none of the payloads APT29 used in these attacks established persistence, allowing a device reboot to stop the malicious activity until visiting a compromised site again.
Regarding its attribution to APT29, Sekoia notes similarities to past watering-hole operations by the same threat group, infrastructure overlaps, and a compromised site that a partner linked to a 2025 APT29 campaign.
Apple and Google have patched all flaws targeted in this campaign, with fixes even reaching older iOS releases , so users are recommended to apply the latest available security updates for their devices.

The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.

articles.title_zh: Gold, silver and precious metals prices jump, dollar dips as Democrats take control of Congress
articles.content_orig:
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning, while the value of the dollar fell, following the U.S. midterm elections.
Spot gold was 2.83% higher at $4,039.59 an ounce by 7:56 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.32% to trade at $51.9235 per ounce.
Front-month gold futures added 2.8% to trade at $4,050.80, while silver futures were up 4.61% at $52.045.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 3.43% to trade at $1,464.60, and palladium, which was 6.21% higher at $991.50.
The moves came as vote counting continued in the midterms, with the Democrats projected to have won control of the House and multiple governors' offices also turning blue.
U.S. stock futures broadly fell as the results came in, while Treasury yields also moved lower . Oil prices were marginally higher, while the U.S. dollar index shed around 0.3%.
Rhona O'Connell, head of market analysis for EMEA and Asia at StoneX, said in a note on Tuesday that if the Democrats won dual Congressional control, gold should find support as rates and the dollar would likely come under pressure.
She said it would result in "fiscal brinkmanship, institutional friction, both leading to uncertainty," adding that "the Iran war and a weaker dollar would compete with [the] impact of [a] hawkish Fed."
"Less fiscal stimulus argues for lower long yields and a softer dollar, offset by debt-limit premia in bills and a Fed leaning towards another hike," she said.
Both gold and silver enjoyed record-breaking rallies in 2025, surging 66% and 135% respectively over the course of the year as investors sought safe haven assets amid geopolitical uncertainty and broader market volatility.
But the momentum has come undone this year, with rising inflation, surging bond yields and hawkish central banks removing support from the metals. Gold is down more than 7% year-to-date, while silver has tumbled almost 28%.
Spot gold rose on Monday as oil prices retreated, and is now on course for a weekly rise of around 3.7%.
Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com, said in a Tuesday note that the recovery remains fragile.
"The challenge for precious metals is that geopolitical uncertainty is not automatically translating into safe-haven demand when investors are also concerned about restrictive monetary policy," she said. "They also face the risk of liquidation during sharp equity selloffs, as investors sell profitable or liquid positions to raise cash."

We tried to address that in length last week, but let’s re-summarize as it is important. In a nutshell, why these reports are misleading:
Let’s just start with an updated version of last weekend’s ( SOX ) (semiconductor index) chart.
Markets initially bounced off of the 200-day moving average, but on Friday, they retested that level and failed. It is often the third retest that is the problem, so a bounce again is quite possible, but breaking the 200-DMA rarely is a good thing.
The Nasdaq 100 is solidly through its 100-DMA and is about 1.6% from testing its own 200-DMA. On Friday, the S&P 500 just broke its 100-DMA for the first time since November 2025. The 200-DMA is 3.5% away on the S&P 500, which should be support.
We are resorting to technicals more than usual because:
From what I see anecdotally and through some simple charts I like to use, the market is not exhibiting strength, and the risk is to further downside.
One positive is credit markets didn’t suffer as badly as stocks on Friday (spreads did not finish at their wides) and none of my indicators for “disorderly” selling pressure have triggered. I am watching those triggers as that is a risk that is still in play.
I remain concerned about the abundance of leveraged ETFs focused on the chip space (with ( SOXL ) being the largest). These amplify moves in both directions. While SOXL had some inflows on Friday, it would have had to sell about $8 billion of stocks into the close, without inflows. This added pressure makes it difficult to separate valuation from mechanically forced buying and selling.
With these indices all potentially exposed to some weak technicals, that makes me very cautious.
The chip sector is crucial for markets and for the economy. A degree of caution seems warranted at the moment, though we have all seen these markets turn on a dime.
I will wait to see how Tuesday plays out. We have become accustomed to polls being inaccurate. Even betting markets failed in Brazil, which we avoided in an otherwise broad cross section of geopolitical risks and opportunities last Monday on CNBC . European stocks did outperform the U.S. last week, despite all the headlines.
I will be watching almost as closely (or more closely) how political leaders respond to the election results. That may be more telling for markets than the results themselves.

Credit outperformed stocks last week. While stocks finished at their lows in many cases, credit was not at the widest levels. This is very good. articles.title_zh: Iran says US reply to Hormuz plan ‘unconvincing’; Trump confirms strikes
articles.content_orig:
Iran has called the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz “unconvincing” as US President Donald Trump confirmed launching strikes on an Iranian island near the strategic waterway.
The developments on Tuesday came as Qatar stepped up diplomatic efforts to avert a renewed war between the US and Iran and as another oil tanker was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz.
The indirect talks centre on an Iranian proposal to reopen the waterway over two days, if the US meets Tehran’s seven demands, including the lifting of sanctions and ending a US naval blockade.
Despite reports of progress in recent days, Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said on Tuesday that Washington’s response had fallen short.
“America’s response to Iran’s rights and demands was not convincing, and they must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them,” he wrote on X.
“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened.”
His post came after Majed al-Ansari, a spokesperson for Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said that talks were continuing and that both sides “remain committed to the negotiation process “.
He said Qatar was facilitating the “real-time exchange of proposals between” the US and Iran.
In Washington, DC, Trump confirmed the US had struck Iran early on Tuesday, telling Fox News that the strikes had targeted an anti-aircraft facility.
He described the operation as a “minor attack” and said it “wasn’t war”.
“They built an anti-aircraft facility. It took them about two months. We watched it get built. As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night,” he said.
Iranian media said the strikes hit Qeshm Island in the Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in the day, US officials told US media that the strikes had been “defensive” and followed Iranian fire at an American aircraft.
The strikes came as US media, citing US officials, reported that Central Command had prepared plans for strikes that could begin as early as Wednesday, after the midterm elections, when three American aircraft carriers would be in the region.
The crucial elections could cost Trump’s Republicans control of both the House and the Senate, and fears have grown that Trump could carry out a threatened attack on Iran once the vote is over.
US media have previously reported that the planned campaign would be short and intense.
Trump meanwhile repeated warnings of further military action on Tuesday, saying, “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people” and “If we have to, we’ll have to.”
In an earlier interview with the Financial Times, he suggested he was content with the state of the stand-off with Iran. “We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute telephone interview.
Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile ordered the military at the weekend to respond to any threat immediately and without geographical limits, and to update its list of targets.
Iranian officials have suggested that European countries and undersea cables in the Gulf could be targeted.
As officials weighed the possibility of escalation, commercial shipping came under further attack .
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed on Wednesday that four oil tankers were destroyed after striking naval mines while attempting to pass through a prohibited shipping lane south of the Strait of Hormuz.
The tankers remained ablaze following the explosions, the IRGC said in a statement carried by the official IRNA news agency. Two other vessels were detained for violating shipping restrictions, it added.
Earlier, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported that two unidentified projectiles struck a tanker’s engine room about 14 nautical miles (26km) northeast of Oman’s coastal village of Limah on Tuesday. No casualties were reported.
It could not be independently verified whether the incidents reported by UKMTO and the IRGC were linked.
The IRGC also claimed its air defence forces shot down a US-made MQ-9 drone over the strait at 4.30am local time (01:00GMT), describing it as the 56th such aircraft it had downed.
The statement said the operations were carried out by the IRGC’s naval and aerospace forces, which had inflicted “heavy blows on the enemy”.
John Mearsheimer, a US political scientist, questioned whether another short bombing campaign could achieve Washington’s objectives, warning that Iranian retaliation could draw the US into a longer confrontation.
“If the 40-day bombing campaign didn’t work, how is the three-day bombing campaign going to work?” he asked in a video commentary, referring to the initial US-Israeli air campaign and proposals for a shorter renewed offensive.
He argued that an Iranian response could prompt further US escalation, increasing the damage to the global economy.

articles.title_zh: Bomb Threats Disrupt Several Flights Across Europe
articles.content_orig:
At least seven flights and a cruise ship in Europe received bomb threats on Tuesday, causing disruption at airports although no devices were discovered.
At least two flights to Warsaw, two to Sofia, two to ​Rome and one to Murcia airport in Spain were subjected to the threats on Tuesday, and another flight to ‌Sofia had been threatened a day earlier. An airport in Warsaw was briefly shut and the Italian Air Force accompanied one of the flights to Rome while an Israel-bound cruise ship was searched for bombs in Greece.
There was no claim of responsibility and officials did not attribute blame. None of the affected airlines responded to Reuters’ requests for comment.
Rhys Jones, Analysis Output Manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, ​said that seven confirmed bomb threats in a single day impacting flights was exceptional.
“The lack of clear target state, airline, or route indicates that general ​disruption to aviation operations is the aim,” Jones told Reuters.
Authorities diverted a LOT flight from London that was meant to land at ​Warsaw’s Chopin airport to nearby Modlin airport, which was closed and then reopened after the plane was searched and ​no device was found.
Another Warsaw-bound flight, an SAS flight from Copenhagen, ​landed at Chopin as scheduled. Chopin airport said no device was found and the airport remained operational.
Bomb threats were made against planes traveling from ​Milan/Bergamo and Dublin to Sofia, Bulgaria’s transport ministry said in a statement to Reuters. Both landed safely and no explosive devices were ​found on inspection.
The Bergamo flight was operated by Wizz Air and was carrying 176 passengers, the statement said. The Dublin flight, operated by Ryanair, had 186 passengers on board.
BTA had earlier quoted an Interior Ministry official as saying a flight from Israel had been impacted, but authorities later said this was ​not the case.
A day earlier, a Wizz Air flight from London to Sofia was diverted to Budapest airport after receiving a bomb threat, Hungarian ​Defence Minister ​Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said ⁠in a Facebook post.
In Murcia in southeastern Spain, parts of an airport were cordoned off on Tuesday after a ‌bomb threat ⁠was reported on a Ryanair flight from Manchester.
Officials said the report proved to be a hoax, and the airport resumed normal operations after authorities found no explosives on board. Ryanair declined to immediately comment.
Two other Ryanair flights – one from Lisbon and another from Dublin – were searched at Rome’s Fiumicino airport following bomb threats, said a source from airport operator ADR. The Dublin flight was escorted by the ​Italian Air Force until it landed.
The ​alert was cleared and the ⁠airport continued to operate as usual with no effects on other flights, the person said.
An ⁠explosives detection dog and a diver searched the Panama-flagged Crown Iris cruise ship on the Greek island of Syros after an unknown person said an explosive device had been attached to the boat’s hull, authorities said.
Initial checks found no explosive device with coast ​guard specialists expected to carry out further inspections before the ship could resume its voyage.
While no country pointed fingers over the bomb threats, they come at a time when European officials have been ​blaming both Russia and Iran for what they describe as “hybrid attacks” and acts of sabotage. Moscow ​and Tehran both ⁠deny any such campaign.
This week, unidentified hackers shut down fridges in supermarkets in several European countries. Some experts said hoax bomb threats could be part of a similar pattern of low-cost, deniable disruption efforts.
“From railways to the food infrastructure that you see happening with the fridges being hacked ⁠and all ​kinds of other operations, it does fit the narrative of Russian state actors ​who want to disturb Europe,” said Eric Schouten, the head of aviation security group Dyami.

SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global stocks slumped and the dollar hit a one-month low on Wednesday as Democrats gained control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, fuelling fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny.
In ‌a major setback to President Donald Trump, Democrats notched up victories in the South Carolina, Texas and Ohio Senate races, capturing majorities in both the ‌Senate and House that reached deep into Republican strongholds.
The breadth of the party's success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard.
AI stocks ​were quick to slide. That in turn put the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies also fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safer assets.
"Tighter regulatory scrutiny of technology and AI companies along with the higher likelihood of political gridlock beckon with a Democrat sweep," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.
The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has ‌left investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the ⁠technology's rapid expansion.
The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
S&P 500 futures were last down 0.35% while Nasdaq futures skidded more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.5%. ⁠European futures were down 0.4%, having slid 1.5% earlier.
"Looks like investors are buying the dip after the initial knee-jerk selloff," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The blue sweep hasn't changed, but markets may be recognising that political gridlock doesn't necessarily mean weaker corporate earnings."
In Asia, the bulk of selling was in AI stocks, with chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC sliding ​sharply ​before cutting losses. The KOSPI was last slightly higher after dropping 3% earlier.
George Efstathopoulos, portfolio manager ​and co-head of multi-asset research at Fidelity International, said he had ‌reduced overall equity exposure and dialled up exposure in defensive sectors like utilities, but thinks now is a good time to gradually rotate back into tech.
"The midterms are a clearing event that can allow investors to focus on sectors where fundamentals and pricing have diverged. Technology is one of them."
INVESTORS RUSH FOR SAFETY OF BONDS
Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending. AI regulation could also slow growth and reduce the need for rate hikes.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/] [US/]
"Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block ‌and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending ​slows," said TD Securities' Newnaha.
Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the Democrats' victory in ​Texas is likely to weigh on chip stocks, raising fears of tighter ​curbs on AI data-centre development in one of the fastest-growing markets for computing infrastructure in the US.
"If Texas declares a moratorium on data ‌centres, as New York did, projects could face further delays," Kim ​said. "Today's market reaction is clearly reflecting concerns ​and uncertainty over these issues."
In currencies, the dollar slid broadly against major peers. The euro rose 0.5% to $1.1249, while sterling firmed 0.37% to $1.3464. That left the dollar index 0.37% lower at 101.34. [FRX/]
The yen and the Swiss franc — both safe-haven currencies — notched up the biggest gains. The yen was 0.7% stronger at 157.55 ​per US dollar, while the Swiss franc firmed almost 0.8% ‌to 0.8144 per US dollar.
In the oil market, prices were choppy on Wednesday after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as ​investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. [O/R]

The Democratic Party is projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press. Democrats securing a sizable majority in the House and Senate — the so-called blue wave scenario — would pressure the market and especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence buildout, according to some on Wall Street. Investors fear a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. AI-linked stocks have already pulled back in recent weeks on concern about a slowing pace in data-center spending.
Big Tech shares Microsoft , Amazon and Nvidia were all trading lower in overnight trading on Robinhood.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.6% on Robinhood, while Tesla shares were down 4.1%. Data center play CoreWeave was down 3.2% in Robinhood overnight trading, while Alphabet was some 0.6% lower.
Equities "trended lower as it's looked more likely that Democrats are going to pick up the House and most likely the Senate," said Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, Tuesday evening as futures were pulling back.

Leveraged traders trimmed holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October
Chinese investors refrained from bets on stocks this week, even as state support unfolded after Beijing unveiled a litany of measures to shore up confidence in the world’s second-largest equity market.
Leveraged traders trimmed their holdings to a one-year low this week, while new stock-account openings dropped by more than 30 per cent in October, according to official data. The retreat in retail enthusiasm contrasted with the government ramping up efforts to prop up stocks, including liquidity injections through two monetary tools and reported suspensions of new share sales to keep a lid on supply.
The divergence illustrates investors’ unease over whether the latest bout of government interventions will drive sustained gains in stocks, which are grappling with weak domestic demand and the fallout of a rout in AI stocks in the US. Investment banks including Bank of America and Macquarie said that state intervention might stabilise sentiment, but would fall short of fuelling a fresh rally.

articles.title_zh: Oil rises on Iran war uncertainty after Trump's Republicans face election rout
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell Tuesday for a second consecutive session, as the market hopes the U.S. and Iran will reach a diplomatic settlement to the conflict that has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures lost 37 cents to close at $96.09 a barrel after dipping below $95 earlier in the session. Brent crude , the international benchmark, shed $1.17 to settle at $103.60.
The move lower came after rumors circulated the U.S. and Iran were making progress toward a deal.
Oil sold off more than 7% on Monday after Washington and Tehran signaled they were both open to discussions to reach a settlement. President Donald Trump told reporters Tehran wants "to make a deal and that could happen."
Qatar is continuing to mediate talks between the U.S. and Iran, the Gulf state's foreign ministry said Tuesday. A delegation from Qatar held talks in Tehran in an effort to reach an agreement that prevents further escalation in the region and ends the U.S.-Iran conflict, the foreign ministry said.
However, Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman Emsaeil Baqaei said Tuesday that Tehran will not accept diplomacy based on coercion, according to the state-owned media outlet Islamic Republic News Agency . It was unclear where talks actual stand.
The market had been pricing in the risk of escalation after the U.S. midterm elections , as reports circulated that Washington was drafting plans for strikes on Iran. Crude prices gained more than 10% in October in response.
The situation in the Middle East remains volatile and there's still substantial risk that fighting could break out. Washington attacked Iran's Qeshm Island on Monday, U.S. officials told The Wall Street Journal, adding that the U.S. has been carrying out "limited strikes" against the country in recent weeks.
The military campaign against Iran has been kept deliberately low-profile to avoid signaling plans for a major escalation in fighting, the report said, quoting an unnamed official.
And commercial ships continue to come under attack in the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman. At least four ship attacks have been reported since the start of the month, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre.
Despite these attacks, the Trump administration has also been touting a possible diplomatic solution to the conflict, with Vice President JD Vance telling CNN, "The president and I both feel really good about the prospect of potentially coming to a negotiated settlement."
On Sunday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
High oil prices have contributed substantially to inflation and high gasoline prices in the U.S., which have become a cause of concern for Trump ahead of the midterm elections.
Last week, two Federal Reserve presidents said interest rates will need to move higher to rein in inflation. Higher rates generally crimp growth and raise costs for consumers, but help to bring down inflation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Canva Announces Layoffs, Job Changes for About 22% of Workforce
articles.content_orig:
Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.
The firm's value has reportedly dropped in the past year over concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on its business as well as the cost of incorporating the technology into its platforms.
It had been "our hardest year yet, and as we shared earlier this year, our growth has slowed for the first time in a decade," Perkins wrote to staff.
The "incredibly hard decision" meant "significant changes," Perkins said.
"For some people, this will mean changes to their roles or being asked to relocate to centralised hubs. Sadly, it will also mean saying goodbye to teammates and friends who have helped build Canva into what it is today."
The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.
Earlier this year two of its backers, Blackbird Ventures and Airtree, reportedly downgraded its valuation from A$60bn ($41.8bn; £31.1bn) at the end of last year to about A$49bn.
Canva also reportedly cut its own internal valuation amid soaring AI expenses related to the roll out of new products.
"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.
The company offers a variety of templates and tools to help users without technical skills or a design background to create a range of professional-looking graphics and presentations, from wedding invitations to business pitch decks.

articles.title_orig: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.title_zh: Google researchers are fighting the company to tell the world what they know about AI
articles.content_orig:
Workers inside Google’s artificial-intelligence division are asking executives to release them from non-disparagement agreements so they can discuss AI’s risks in public, The Washington Post reported. The request puts a plain question in front of one of the world’s most powerful AI employers: who gets to speak when the people closest to the technology think the public deserves a warning?
The reported dispute involves employees at Google DeepMind, including staff in London. A contract reviewed by The Washington Post reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, including after they leave Google. Two current Google DeepMind workers told the paper that the agreements restrict public communication about AI’s potential impacts.
Google has pushed back on part of the picture. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A Google spokesperson added that the company does not enforce such clauses after employees leave and provides internal channels for escalating concerns. Disclosure pressure on AI labs is rising on several fronts, and our look at what the Anthropic amended S-1 disclosed on November 2 shows how much a lab now has to tell investors. This story asks the mirror-image question: how much can its workers tell everyone else?

Four points hold up in the reporting available to us. First, workers in Google’s AI division are asking executives for release from non-disparagement agreements. Second, the dispute concerns Google DeepMind staff, including people based in London. Third, a contract The Washington Post reviewed reportedly bars some British employees from criticizing the company for life, even after they leave. Fourth, two current DeepMind workers said the agreements limit what they can say publicly about AI’s possible impacts.
Those are the load-bearing facts. Everything else around this story, including some of the headline phrasing that has circulated, goes further than the record does. The idea that Google researchers are collectively demanding the freedom to tell the world what they know about AI is a fair summary of the mood, but it is not independently established beyond the worker requests The Washington Post described. We have no verified count of participating researchers, no list of signatories, and no named organizer.
We also have no on-record quote from a named Google DeepMind researcher in the material available for this report. That matters for how much weight readers should put on any single claim. The two current workers appear in the reporting as sources describing the agreements, not as named spokespeople for a movement. A story built on a reviewed contract and two employees is still news, but it is a narrower story than a walkout or an open letter would be.
One detail deserves attention. The workers are reported to be asking executives to release them, which is a request, not a breach. That choice signals that at least some staff want to stay inside the rules while changing them. It also suggests they see the contract language, not company culture, as the obstacle.
A non-disparagement clause is a contract term that limits what a person can say publicly about their employer. Standard versions cover false or damaging statements. Broader versions can reach honest criticism, opinions, and even neutral descriptions of internal decisions if the wording is loose enough. Companies use them to protect reputation, and employees often sign them as part of an offer letter or a separation package without reading the fine print twice.
The difference between a narrow clause and a broad one is the whole story here. A narrow clause leaves room for a worker to say that a safety process failed or that a product carries a risk the public should weigh. A broad one makes the worker think twice before saying anything at all. When the subject is AI risk, a field where insiders often know things outsiders cannot check, that chilling effect carries real cost.
The reported contract goes beyond a standard employment-period restriction. According to The Washington Post, it bars some British employees from criticizing Google for life, including after they leave. A restriction that survives employment has no natural end date. A researcher who quits after five years of safety work would stay bound in year ten, even if the technology and the risks look nothing like they did at signing.
Note the qualifier in the reporting: the reviewed contract covers some British employees, not every DeepMind worker. We do not know the exact language used across the workforce, and the reporting does not claim a single uniform clause. Any reader judging Google’s conduct should keep that gap in view.
Google answered with two statements. The company said it updated terms for new hires to remove the post-termination portion of non-disparagement clauses. A spokesperson also said Google does not enforce non-disparagement clauses after employees leave, and that the company provides internal channels for people to escalate concerns.
Both statements carry weight, and both leave questions open. Removing the post-termination portion for new hires is a concrete contract change. It tells us Google’s lawyers saw enough risk or enough pressure to rewrite the template. A non-enforcement pledge is softer. It describes what the company does today, not what the paper allows tomorrow.
That distinction explains why employees are reported to be seeking clearer legal protection through revised contract language. A worker deciding whether to speak at a conference or give a journalist a background interview does not rely on a spokesperson’s description of enforcement habits. They rely on the text they signed. If the text says one thing and the practice says another, the safest move for the individual is silence.
Internal escalation channels address a different problem. They give employees a place to raise concerns inside the company, which helps when management listens. They do nothing for a worker who has raised concerns internally, seen no change, and now wants the public to know. The workers’ request, as reported, targets that second situation.
Google’s stated fix applies to new hires. The reporting we have does not say whether current employees, or people who already left under older terms, get the same change. That gap is the center of the dispute. A policy that improves the paperwork for the next cohort leaves the people who raised the issue on the old terms.
Several questions follow, and none has a confirmed answer in the available reporting:
Each question has a simple yes or no answer that Google could publish. The company’s decision on whether to answer them will say more about its posture than the original contract language did.
News about AI labs moves fast and headlines tend to outrun facts. The table below separates what the reporting supports from what it does not, so readers can see where the evidence stops.
Two lessons come out of that table. The core facts are solid because they rest on a document the paper reviewed and on company statements. The movement framing is softer, and readers should treat it as interpretation until someone names organizers or publishes a letter.
The reported contract covers British employees, and DeepMind has a major presence in London. That puts the dispute inside a country with its own regulators, its own employment rules, and its own public conversation about AI. UK officials have been vocal about AI risk in other domains. Our earlier report on the NCSC warning that AI malware could hit UK critical infrastructure within two years shows how seriously British security agencies treat the subject.
A government that asks the public to take AI risk seriously will find it awkward when the people who build the technology say they cannot

articles.title_zh: Midterm election results 2026: Who’s winning and what’s at stake for stocks and the economy
articles.content_orig:

Control of the US Congress is the prize on November 3, 2026, as Democrats attempt to wrest majorities from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Voters will also choose governors in 36 of the 50 states, and nearly every state will hold elections for its state-level legislative bodies.
Ballots have been cast for weeks, with early voting underway across the country ahead of Election Day .
The midterms , held in the middle of each four-year presidential term, by definition do not involve the president himself.
But anyone tempted to dismiss this year's contests as lacking drama or importance should weigh two statistics.
More than 100 million people are expected to cast ballots in this year's midterm voting, if turnout is anything like the previous midterm in 2022.
And as of October 30, a record $11.6 billion had been spent on political advertisements for the 2025–26 election cycle.
AdImpact, which tracks the activities, said the top spending is in battleground US Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.
Campaign finance records show Elon Musk alone has spent $442 million to support Republicans.
Midterms generally attract fewer voters than the higher-profile presidential races.
For example, more than 155 million votes were cast in the 2024 presidential election.
In the House, Republicans currently hold a 218-214 majority, with two vacancies and one independent who caucuses with Republicans.
Democrats must win a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber.
The Senate is also in play, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority.
Democrats must net four additional seats to get control there.
Ten races, including those in Maine, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa and Georgia, could decide the outcome.
Trump's approval of his performance is at an all-time low of 32 percent, according to a September Reuters/Ipsos poll.
Domestic issues like rising consumer prices are likely to affect the outcome of many races and could erode support for Republicans.
Evidence suggests Democrats are more enthusiastic about voting this year than Republicans.
If early voting trends continue, it could point to a Democratic win in November.
There are also signs that Latino voters who veered to Trump in 2024 might be returning to Democrats because of frustration over the economy and some of Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.
A landslide for the Democrats, however, is far from assured.
Republicans could benefit from continued skepticism toward Democrats, a Republican spending advantage in campaigns, and fears among moderate voters over some primary wins by left-wingers.
Midterm elections generally are dangerous territory for the political party that holds the White House and/or Congress.
For 2026, that means Trump and his Republicans controlling the US Senate and House of Representatives are in perilous political positions.
The midterms can be an opportunity for voters to, in effect, grade the president's performance, and possibly trigger White House course corrections if they receive low marks.
Midterm election results can also give aspiring presidential candidates hints on how to tailor their messages to voters in the next presidential campaign, which in this case will be in 2028.
Recent history shows the shockwaves a midterm election can produce.
In the 2010 midterms, during Barack Obama's Democratic presidency, Republicans scored major victories, winning 63 additional House seats amid an underperforming US economy and weak support for Obama's landmark healthcare reform legislation.
Democrats lost their majority.
In the Senate, they held onto control despite losing six seats.
The Republican wave was a "shellacking," Obama lamented at the time.
He subsequently faced Republican demands for significant reductions to non-defense spending.
Democrats returned the favor in 2018, with Trump in the White House.
They gained a net 40 House seats but lost a net two Senate seats.
At the state level, Republicans currently control 55% of state legislative seats across the country, while Democrats hold 43.8%, according to Ballotpedia.
If Democrats manage to win the House, the next speaker — second in line for the presidency after the vice president — is likely to be Democratic Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
He is currently the House Democratic leader.
Jeffries, who would become the first Black American to hold the powerful office, would be in a position to direct House committees to investigate a range of controversial activities by Trump and his associates.
Jeffries has repeatedly said Democrats would look into what he has called "unprecedented levels of corruption" during the Trump administration.
Jeffries also would steer Democrats' legislative priorities through the House.
He has said Democrats would focus on making healthcare, groceries, housing, energy and other costs more affordable.
A Republican win, on the other hand, would ensure that the speaker's gavel remains in that party's hands, either with current speaker Mike Johnson or whichever Republican prevails if he is challenged for the job.
Republican priorities are likely to be focused on additional tax cuts, huge increases in defense spending, and deeper social safety net reductions, building on Trump's 2025 "One Big Beautiful Bill."
Among the most-watched House races are Republican Representative Mike Lawler's bid for reelection to a New York district that Democratic candidate Kamala Harris won in her 2024 presidential campaign.
An open seat in a Nebraska swing district, where farmers and truckers face sharply higher fuel prices as a result of the US war against Iran, is also drawing attention.
Also high on Democrats' list of House seats they hope to take from Republicans are two in Pennsylvania and one in New Jersey.
Hovering over all of this are questions over whether Trump will try to meddle in the elections, which are administered by the 50 individual states.
Since 2020, he has repeatedly insisted there is widespread cheating in US elections, despite a lack of evidence.
State election officials and Democrats in Congress have been preparing for possible legal challenges to any moves by his administration to try to intervene.
There is no set time for when the world will learn the results of the US midterm elections.
In tight races, winners may not be called for days or even weeks.
The first individual race calls are expected to start after polls begin to close in the United States on Tuesday night, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. (ET) (2300 GMT).
Polls then close in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4).
The last polls to close are in far western Alaska at 1 a.m. ET.
